summary: Jon Postel's revised list of standard host names, which tries to match the names used by the Network Information Center. He also gives a four-character alternate list, noting that programmers like short names made of simple characters. It replaced RFC 229.

eli5.summary: Another try at a list of nicknames for network computers. This one has a longer version and a short four-letter version, because programmers like short names.

questions: who proposed standard host names arpanet
subtitle: Jon Postel's revised list of standard ARPANET host names, with a short four-character alternate for each.

tldr.problem: The network had no agreed names for its hosts, and earlier lists in RFC 226 and RFC 229 disagreed on name length.
tldr.mechanism: Postel restates his list of standard names, keeps them consistent with the Network Information Center's site names where possible, and adds an alternate list limited to 4 characters of capital letters and digits.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 229 and was itself followed by further proposals such as RFC 247 and RFC 273.

today: RFC 236 obsoletes RFC 229 and was followed by other proposals, including RFC 247 and RFC 273. Its metadata does not record it as obsoleted.

sections.title: Earlier Proposals
sections.content:
In RFC 226, Peggy Karp suggested a set of standard host names, 6 characters long, and gave a partial list. In RFC 229, Jon Postel suggested 8 character names and gave a longer list. This RFC presents that list again with some modifications.

Postel suggests that standard names be consistent with the site names used by the Network Information Center as far as possible, and that each host's technical liaison officer be consulted before a name is assigned.
sections.eli5: Two people had already suggested name lists. This is a tweaked second try that tries to match the names the information office already uses.

sections.title: The Alternate Short Names
sections.content:
Postel notes that programmers are lazy and do not like character strings longer than one computer word or containing anything other than the capital letters A-Z or the digits 0-9. So he adds an alternate list limited to 4 character names using only those alphanumerics.

For example, site 1 is UCLA-NMC with alternate NMC, and site 2 is SRI-ARC with alternate NIC.
sections.eli5: Long names are a pain to type. So each computer also gets a short four-letter name that is easy to work with.

sections.title: The Name Table
sections.content:
The table gives each numbered site a standard name and an alternate name. It runs from site 1 (UCLA-NMC, alternate NMC) through entries such as BBN-NCC, MIT-DMCG, RAND-65 and SU-AI, to site 158, BBN-TIP, with alternate BBNT.

Names ending in TIP are used for terminal IMP sites such as AMES-TIP and NBS-TIP.
sections.eli5: The table is a phone book: a number, a long name and a short name for each site.

references.text: Karp, P., proposal for standard host names, RFC 226.
